summary: Gives the problem statement for the Interface to Network Security Functions work and some companion use cases. It sets out why a standard interface for managing security functions, such as firewalls, is needed.

plainLanguage.summary: A network security function is any box or program that protects the network: a firewall, an intrusion detector, a VPN gateway. Each is programmed in its own vendor's way, so a provider who wants to mix several products has to write special code for each one. This document sets out why that is a problem and what a common interface would have to do.

subtitle: Why the industry wants one way to program firewalls and other security boxes, whoever made them.

tldr.problem: Companies are moving their firewalls, intrusion detection and other security functions into the provider's network, but each vendor's equipment is programmed through its own private interface, so every provider writes custom code for every product.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes the problem in detail: no standard interface to control and monitor security functions, no way to describe what a given product can do, no way to feed it new signatures, and no way to hand out keys.
tldr.outcome: The result is a statement of what an interface to network security functions has to solve, together with the use cases it has to serve, from access networks to cloud data centres and regulatory audits.

today: RFC 8192 is an Informational document published in July 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a problem statement, not a specification: the interfaces it describes are developed in the companion I2NSF documents, and it requires no IANA actions.

sections.title: Why Security Functions Are Moving Out of the Building
sections.content:
The growing challenges and complexity of maintaining a secure infrastructure, complying with regulatory requirements and controlling costs are enticing enterprises into consuming network security functions hosted by service providers. The hosted security service is especially attractive to small and medium-size enterprises, which suffer from a lack of security experts to continuously monitor networks, acquire new skills and propose immediate mitigations to ever increasing sets of security attacks.

Demand for hosted, or cloud-based, security services is growing. Small and medium-size businesses are increasingly adopting cloud-based security services to replace on-premises security tools, while larger enterprises are deploying a mix of traditional and cloud-based security services. To meet that demand, more and more service providers are providing hosted security solutions to deliver cost-effective managed security services to enterprise customers. As a result, network security functions are provided and consumed in a large variety of environments, and users may consume security services hosted by their own enterprise, by service providers, or by a combination of both.

The document sets out the problem statement for the Interface to Network Security Functions work and outlines some use cases, and it notes that a summary of the state of the art in the industry and in the IETF is documented separately.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies that cannot afford a team of security specialists are handing the job to a provider. The provider's own staff then have to work with whatever boxes they have, and the boxes all behave differently.

sections.title: The Basic Framework: Client, Controller, Security Function
sections.content:
Standard interfaces for monitoring and controlling the behaviour of security functions are essential building blocks for security service providers and enterprises to automate the use of different security functions from multiple vendors. I2NSF may be invoked by any authorized client, and examples of authorized clients are upstream applications, controllers, orchestration systems and security portals.

Users request security services through specific clients, such as a customer application, the business and operations support systems of a network service provider, or a management platform. The appropriate network entity then invokes the security functions according to the user's service request, and this network entity is called the security controller.

There are two interfaces. Interface 1 is used for receiving security requirements from a client and translating them into commands that the security functions can understand and execute; the security controller also passes back the security reports it has gathered from the security functions to the client. Interface 2 is used for interacting with the security functions according to those commands, for example enacting or revoking a security policy or distributing a policy, and for collecting status information about them.

Client devices or applications can require the security controller to add, delete or update rules in the security service function for their specific traffic. When users want the executing status of a security service, they can request it from the client, and the security controller collects the information through Interface 2, consolidates it and gives the feedback to the client through Interface 1. That interface can also collect aggregated data suitable for tasks such as infrastructure security assessment.

Customers may require validating the availability, provenance and execution of a security function. This validation, especially relevant to virtual security functions, includes at least the integrity of the function, that it is not compromised; isolation, so that its execution is self-contained for privacy requirements in multi-tenancy scenarios; and provenance, giving strict guarantees about the origin of the function, its status such as available, idle or down, and feedback mechanisms so a customer can check that the function conforms to their requirements. To achieve this the security controller may collect security measurements and share them with an independent and trusted third party through Interface 1, so that the third party can attest to the functions. This implies two types of clients on Interface 1, the end user and the trusted third party, and the I2NSF work may determine that Interface 1 creates two sub-interfaces to support them.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parties are involved. A client asks for security service, a security controller turns that request into instructions and collects the results, and the security functions do the actual work. The controller talks to clients on one interface and to the security functions on another, and it can also hand measurements to an outside trusted party so they can check the functions are genuine.

sections.title: The Challenges Facing Service Providers
sections.content:
There are many types of network security function, and those from different vendors can have different features and interfaces, deployed in multiple locations with different roles. The examples the document gives include external intrusion and attack protection, such as firewall and access control list authentication, intrusion protection and detection systems and endpoint protection; functions in a demilitarized zone, such as firewalls, intrusion detection and protection, AAA services, NAT, forwarding proxies and application filtering; centralized or distributed security functions; internal security analysis and reporting, such as security logs, event correlation and forensic analysis; internal data and content protection, such as encryption, authorization and key management for internal databases; and security gateways and VPN concentrators.

Given that diversity, standardizing all aspects of security functions is challenging and probably not feasible, and fortunately it is not necessary. From an I2NSF perspective there is no need to standardize how every firewall's filtering is created or applied, because some features may be unique to a vendor's product. What is needed is a standardized interface to control and monitor the rule sets that security functions use to treat packets.

Several specific gaps follow from that. Since no widely accepted industry standard interface to security functions exists today, management of the functions, including device and policy provisioning and monitoring, tends to be custom-made security management offered by product vendors, so automation of such services, if it exists at all, is also custom made. A function cannot monitor what it cannot view, so enabling a function to mitigate an intrusion must include a mechanism to provide monitoring feedback in order to determine that the intrusion has stopped, and an industry standard interface could provide monitoring across a variety of functions.

The functions are also becoming virtual and distributed. A virtual security function has a higher risk of changes to the state of network connection, interfaces or traffic, because the virtual machines hosting them are created, moved or decommissioned, and the ETSI Network Functions Virtualization initiative creates new management challenges for security policies enforced by distributed virtual functions.

Further demands are listed in the document. More clients, applications or controllers need to update their security policies dynamically. Providers may need several controllers to control and monitor functions, especially once they are distributed and virtualised. There is no standard method for vendors to describe the capabilities of their security functions, even within one product category, so a provider's management system has no way to retrieve what a given function supports; dynamic capability registration is useful because security functions may be subject to software and hardware updates that affect the policies they enforce. Many security functions depend on signature files or profiles, such as intrusion detection signatures and DDoS filters, and there is no standard envelope, that is, a message format, to let them use external profiles. There is no mechanism for accepting external alerts that trigger automatic rule and configuration changes, such as a DDoS alert triggering a change to the routing system so that traffic goes to a scrubbing service. And there is no standard interface for provisioning and managing security associations, even though many key management methods and cryptographic suites exist.
sections.plainLanguage: The trouble is that security functions are not alike and are not talked to in the same way. Each product has its own management software, so anything automated is custom-made too. On top of that the functions are moving into virtual machines that can be moved or switched off, nothing says what a given product can actually do, there is no standard way to hand a function a fresh list of attack signatures or to tell it that an attack has started, and no standard way to give it the keys it needs.

sections.title: The Challenges Facing Customers
sections.content:
When customers invoke hosted security services, their security policies may be enforced by a collection of security functions hosted in different domains. Customers may not have the security skills to express sufficiently precise requirements, and usually they express the expectations of their security requirements or the intent of their security policies. They may also desire to express guidelines for security management, such as which critical communications are to be preserved during critical events and which hosts will continue to offer services over the network, what signalling information is passed to a controller during a DDoS in order to ask for mitigation services, reporting of attacks to a CERT, and managing network connectivity of systems out of compliance.

Many medium and large enterprises have deployed on-premises security functions that they want to continue to use, and want to combine local functions with remote hosted ones to achieve more efficient and immediate countermeasures to attacks from both the Internet and the enterprise network. Some may only need hosted services for their remote branch offices where minimal security infrastructure exists.

Customers may use functions provided by multiple service providers, and need to express their security requirements, guidelines and expectations to those providers, who must then translate that information into customer security policies and associated configuration tasks for the set of functions in their network. Without a standardized interface that provides a clear technical characterization, the provider faces several problems. There is no standard technical characterization, API or interface, even for the most common security services; most are accessible only through disparate proprietary interfaces, such as portals or APIs, in whatever format the vendor chooses, so the provider must process the customer's input through widely varying interfaces and differing configuration models. Without a standard interface, new security products find a large barrier to entry to the market. Customers may also require a mechanism to update or modify their security requirements with immediate effect in the underlying functions. Security functions may be solicited without an explicit invocation means, though some may be required to interact with a service function. And current practice relies on scripts that generate other scripts, which automatically run to upload or download configuration changes and log information; those scripts have to be adjusted each time a different vendor's technology is enabled by a provider.

Customers also need ways to monitor the delivered security service. How a policy is translated into technology-specific actions is hidden from them, yet they want to know which policies are in effect, how many attacks are being prevented and how much bandwidth the enforcement costs. Today there is no standard way to get these details, and so there is no way to assure customers that their specified policies are properly enforced by the functions in the provider's domain. They also want the information to run what-if scenarios with real data, and a tight loop between the data gathered and the planning can reduce the time it takes to design and deploy workable policies.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer's side is just as awkward. They say what they want in their own words, the provider has to turn that into rules for a particular product, and the customer cannot afterwards see which rules are actually in force or whether the service is doing anything. They also cannot ask for a change and have it take effect at once without going through the provider's own interface.

sections.title: Where the Work Is Aimed
sections.content:
In the access network scenario, users such as residential, enterprise and mobile users request and manage security services hosted in the provider's infrastructure, connected through virtual access nodes such as the virtual customer premises equipment, the virtual provider edge and the virtual evolved packet core. Residential users ask for parental control, content management and threat management, where threat management includes identifying and blocking botnets or malware. Enterprise users ask for flow security policies and managed security services, with flow policies identifying and blocking malicious activity during access to websites or social media applications, and managed services covering detection and mitigation of external and internal threats such as application or phishing attacks, malware, botnets and DDoS. Service providers ask for policies that protect their own networks against DDoS, botnets and malware, and these policies also enforce isolation between multiple tenants. Mobile users ask for quality of experience monitoring, content management, parental controls and external threat management. Some access customers do not care which functions are used, so the provider's orchestration systems can select them internally; others, especially some enterprise customers, contract separately for dedicated virtual functions, which involves deploying the function on a network functions virtualisation infrastructure, then enrolling and cancelling the customer's subscription, configuring the function from specific configurations or from common policies defined by the provider, and retrieving the function's capabilities from a manifest or descriptor so the provider's management systems can offer detailed information through commercial channels.

In the cloud data centre scenario, firewalls may need to be dynamically added or removed, either at the user's request or when a pre-agreed demand level in the service level agreement is reached, for example adding firewall capacity when bandwidth utilisation hits a threshold for a period of time. The dynamic nature of delivery encourages the security devices to be in software or virtual form rather than physical appliances, and new instances need to be placed in the right zone, which matters for multi-tenant environments and for organisations with their own segregation policies. It is often not feasible to deploy dedicated physical firewalls for each client, so virtual firewalls are deployed dynamically for each client's servers. Firewall rules are tied to addresses and ports, and clients of cloud data centres only see virtual networks and virtual addresses, which may differ from the actual packets traversing the firewalls; even though most vendors support similar firewall features, the specific rule configuration keywords differ from vendor to vendor, which makes automation difficult.

Other use cases cover preventing DDoS, malware and botnet attacks, where the framework should provide a client-side interface that is use case independent and technology agnostic, so that security policy configuration can look for specific malware signatures or prevent access to botnet command and control servers. And regulatory and compliance policies: organisations subject to regulations such as the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard or the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act must isolate kinds of traffic and show records of their security policies whenever audited, and the security controller could keep track of when and where a specific policy was applied, providing that information as proof of compliance.
sections.plainLanguage: The document works through where this would be used: providers offering security to homes, businesses and mobile users; data centres that add and remove firewalls as demand changes and where customers cannot see the rules that apply to them; stopping attacks by blocking malware and botnet sites; and showing an auditor that a policy was in force at a given time and place.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Secure access to control and monitor security functions is crucial for hosted security services. A security controller raises new security threats: it needs to be resilient to attacks and to recover from them quickly, so proper secure communication channels have to be carefully specified for the traffic that carries, controls and monitors the functions and their management entities.

The traffic flow security policies specified by customers can conflict with the provider's internal policies. The conflict can be resolved in one of two ways: installed policies can restrict traffic if either the customer's policies or the provider's internal policies restrict it, or they can restrict traffic only if both do. Either choice could cause problems, and it is crucial for the management system to flag these conflicts to the customers and to the service provider. It is also important to perform proper AAA to authorize access to the network and to the I2NSF management stream.

Enforcing the appropriate privacy is key to all IETF protocols, and is especially important for security management protocols since they are deployed to protect the network. In some circumstances such protocols may be used to protect an individual's home, phone or other personal data, and any solution should carefully consider whether combining management streams abides by the recommendations for data minimization, user participation and security.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller that programs security boxes is itself a target, so the links to it have to be protected and it has to survive an attack. Two sets of rules, the customer's and the provider's, can contradict each other, and the management system has to point that out rather than pick one silently. And because the same management protocol may be watching a person's private data, privacy has to be handled deliberately.

items.text: A virtual function's host machines can be created, moved or decommissioned, changing the state of connections and traffic.

items.text: There is no standard method for a vendor to describe the capabilities of its security functions.

items.text: There is no standard envelope for the profiles and signature files that security functions depend on.

items.title: No way to hand out keys
items.text: There is no standard interface to provision and manage the security associations between the pieces.
